title: By your grace
hookLine: the heading means by Your grace; ten verses follow

lines: A BOWL OF WARM KARAH PRASAD.
cards: Stand in line at a gurdwara near the end of the service and watch people's hands. A sevadar comes down the row with a bowl of warm karah prasad, the sweet made of flour, ghee and sugar.
Nobody reaches in and takes a scoop. Each person holds out two cupped hands, and a spoonful is placed in them. Even a toddler learns it: hands together, open, waiting.
You don't earn it at the counter. You receive it. The next bani of the Sikh morning has that same word written over its door.

teach.b: Tav prasad. Tav means your; prasad means grace, a gift freely given.

teach.h: THE SAME PRASAD AS THE SWEET.
teach.b: It's the same prasad as the sweet in your hands, and the same word that closes the Mool Mantar: gur prasad, by the Guru's grace.
Guru Gobind Singh writes tav prasad as a heading again and again, over section after section, like a dedication at the top of every page. Here it heads ten short poems, the Tav Prasad Savaiye.
A savaiya is a verse form of four long, swinging lines, made for reciting aloud.
These ten come from the Tenth Guru's Akal Ustat, the praise of the Timeless One, written in Braj, a literary language of north India in his day.
Sikhs who keep Nitnem say them every morning, right after the Jaap, and they're among the five banis recited while the amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation. Here's the surprise.
After a heading like by your grace, you'd expect soft, comforting verses.

Instead the ten savaiye march past everything people in the Guru's world admired: ascetics and yogis, elephants hung with gold, emperors with beating drums, pilgrims at every river, rituals of every kind.
After each parade, the verses set it all down and say, in effect, that without the Lord's love and grace it weighs nothing. So the heading is the key.

teach.h: A PARADE OF WHAT PEOPLE ADMIRE.
teach.b: Everything below it is what people try to achieve; the heading names what can only be received.
Over the next week, the parade, one float at a time.

how: Many Sikhs recite the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning after Jaap Sahib, and they are among the five banis read while amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation.

o: by your grace, a gift received
for your sake, an offering made
by your order, a command obeyed

games.q: by your grace — tap the pairs.
p: a verse form of four long lines
the praise of the Timeless One

s: the prasad in tav prasad is the same word as karah prasad, the gurdwara sweet
both mean grace, a gift given freely. the sweet is received in open hands.
the Tav Prasad Savaiye are in the Guru Granth Sahib
they are by Guru Gobind Singh and come from his Akal Ustat, in the Dasam Granth.
the ten savaiye are only read privately, never at the Khalsa initiation
they are among the five banis recited while the amrit is prepared.

games.q: you're at the gurdwara and a sevadar comes down the row with a bowl of warm karah prasad. what do you do?
o: reach into the bowl and take a scoop.
hold out two cupped hands and receive it.
wave it away, since you didn't help make it.
games.why: the custom is two cupped hands, open and waiting. prasad means grace: it is placed in your hands, not taken.

practice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up and a little cupped, the way people hold them for karah prasad.
Notice three things you're holding right now that you didn't make: the breath going in, the light in the room, the fact that you woke up today. If you pray, whisper Waheguru as each one lands.

wordCard.voice: Tav prasad, by your grace: the heading the Tenth Guru writes over these ten verses, from the same prasad as the gurdwara's sweet and the Japji's gur prasad.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: by your grace. the heading Guru Gobind Singh writes over these ten verses and many of his others.

carryVoice: Your line: cupped hands, waiting. Grace is received, never taken or earned. Until tomorrow, then.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, Nitnem and the Amrit ceremony
